title: Squiggle normal form for the nerve-enriched free adjunction
statement:
Use simplicial sets and ordinary nerves of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. A simplicial category has simplicial mapping sets and strictly associative unital simplicial composition. Let $\mathsf{Adj}$ be the homwise nerve of the free strict $2$-category on $\ell:+\to-$, $u:-\to+$, $\eta:1_+\Rightarrow u\ell$, $\epsilon:\ell u\Rightarrow1_-$, subject to $(\epsilon\ell)(\ell\eta)=1_\ell$ and $(u\epsilon)(\eta u)=1_u$.

There is an isomorphism of simplicial categories, fixing objects and these generators, with the following string model. An $n$-arrow is a nonempty finite string $a=(a_0,\ldots,a_w)$ in the ordered alphabet $-<1<\cdots<n<+$, with both endpoints in $\{-,+\}$, and with successive inequalities strictly alternating: if $a_0=-$, then $a_i<a_{i+1}$ for even $i$ and $a_i>a_{i+1}$ for odd $i$; reverse these inequalities if $a_0=+$. The source is $a_w$, target $a_0$, and width is $w$. The singleton strings are identities. Composition is concatenation at the common endpoint, retaining it only once. Identify the alphabet with $[n+1]$ by $-=0$, $+=n+1$. A face $d_i$ applies the monotone map $[n+1]\to[n]$ identifying $i$ and $i+1$ to every letter and then deletes consecutive equal pairs until strictly alternating; the reduced result is independent of deletion order. A degeneracy $s_i$ applies the injection $[n+1]\to[n+2]$ omitting $i+1$. These formulas satisfy the simplicial identities and preserve composition. The strings for $\ell,u,\eta,\epsilon,\beta$ are respectively $(-,+),(+,-),(+,1,+),(-,1,-),(-,2,1,+)$, where $\beta$ has faces $d_2\beta=\ell\eta$, $d_1\beta=s_0\ell$, $d_0\beta=\epsilon\ell$.

A nonidentity arrow is atomic (has no factorization into two nonidentity arrows) exactly when its interior contains neither endpoint symbol. A string is nondegenerate exactly when each of $1,\ldots,n$ occurs. Every arrow has a unique expression as a composable word of degeneracies of nondegenerate atomic arrows, with the unique order-preserving surjection specifying each degeneracy; identities are empty words. In particular each degree is a free category on its atomic arrows, and degeneracies preserve atomicity. Every nondegenerate nonidentity $n$-arrow has $n<w$; for each fixed width there are only finitely many nondegenerate strings, allowing all dimensions.

source.place: Definitions 3.1.2, 3.1.3, 3.1.8; Observations 3.1.4--3.1.9; Proposition 3.1.10, Example 3.1.11, and Corollary 3.3.5 (pp. 816--829); finite-width observation in Proposition 4.2.15 Read online; archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag states this combinatorial result.

proof.text: Use the nerve convention of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. First construct the proposed string category $W$ independently of the free adjunction. Write $W_n$ for its strings in degree $n$. Concatenating at a common endpoint preserves strict alternation: at $-$ the entering inequality is decreasing and the departing one increasing, and at $+$ the reverse holds. Retaining this endpoint once makes concatenation associative, since either parenthesization gives the same list of letters. The singleton at either endpoint is a two-sided identity. Source and target are respectively the last and first letters.

Let $R$ denote adjacent-equal-pair deletion. It terminates because length decreases by two. Uniqueness of the irreducible result follows by induction on length: two possible first deletions either coincide, are disjoint (perform both, in either order), or overlap in $xxx$ (both give $x$ in that position). Apply the induction hypothesis to the shorter resulting strings and to their common descendant. In a weakly alternating string, deleting an equal pair preserves weak alternation, since the indices after that pair change by two and comparison across the gap uses the equal letters. The endpoint symbols are retained as values: the initial and final runs at an extreme have odd length, and if they meet the whole constant string has odd length. Thus reduction of the image of a valid string under an endpoint-preserving monotone map is nonempty, has the original endpoint signs, and is strictly alternating when no equal pair remains. This also covers singleton strings.

source.place: Definition 3.1.8, p. 820; expanded termination and overlap argument

proof.text: For a monotone $\alpha:[m]\to[n]$, define its interval map by $I\alpha(j)=\#\{i\in[m]:\alpha(i)<j\}$ for $0\leq j\leq n+1$. It is monotone, fixes the bottom and top signs, and $I(\alpha\gamma)=I\gamma\circ I\alpha$: the indices $i$ satisfying $\alpha(i)<j$ form the initial segment of length $I\alpha(j)$, so $\alpha(\gamma(k))<j$ is equivalent to $\gamma(k)<I\alpha(j)$. Define $a\cdot\alpha=R((I\alpha)_*a)$. Entrywise application sends an equal pair to an equal pair, hence $R(f_*R(b))=R(f_*b)$ by uniqueness from step 2. Consequently $(a\cdot\alpha)\cdot\gamma=a\cdot(\alpha\gamma)$, and the identity acts identically. The interval maps of $\delta^i$ and $\sigma^i$ are respectively the surjection identifying $i,i+1$ and the injection omitting $i+1$; this gives exactly the stated faces and degeneracies and all simplicial identities.

source.place: Observation 3.1.7 and Definition 3.1.8, pp. 819--820; interval formula expanded

proof.text: These operators preserve composition. Indeed a monotone endpoint-preserving letter map sends the retained junction to the same endpoint; reduce the two pieces on their own, keeping one representative of their odd-length endpoint runs at the junction. Each deletion removes two copies and therefore has the same effect in the joined string. Conversely reductions crossing that junction only remove pairs in this same endpoint run; its odd parity leaves the retained common endpoint. Uniqueness of reduction gives $R(f_*(b\circ a))=R(f_*b)\circ R(f_*a)$. Identity strings are fixed. We have therefore constructed a simplicial category $W$ with precisely the formulas in the statement.

source.place: Definition 3.1.8, p. 820; compatibility with composition expanded

proof.text: Cut a nonidentity string at every interior occurrence of $-$ or $+$. Each piece has no such occurrence, and any factorization into nonidentity arrows must cut at one of these positions, since composition retains exactly the shared endpoint. This proves both the characterization of atoms and the unique atomic word, in every degree. A degeneracy only relabels letters by an injective endpoint-preserving map, so it introduces no new endpoint occurrence and preserves atomicity. An arrow is in the image of $s_i$ precisely when its string omits $i+1$: one direction follows from the omitted value, and in the other direction decrease all letters greater than $i+1$ by one to obtain its unique preimage. Thus nondegeneracy is exactly occurrence of every internal letter.

For each atomic factor, list its distinct internal letters as $j_1<\cdots<j_r$ and replace $j_t$ by $t$, keeping the endpoint signs. This produces a nondegenerate atomic $r$-arrow. The original factor is its degeneracy: the interval injection sends $0$ to $0$, $t$ to $j_t$, and $r+1$ to $n+1$. The corresponding surjection $[n]\to[r]$ is explicitly $i\mapsto\#\{t:j_t\leq i\}$, so is unique. Conversely any degeneracy of a nondegenerate factor has exactly this numerical support and hence this surjection. Combine with the unique cuts of step 5. Identities give empty words. This proves the full unique expression asserted, not just degreewise freeness.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.10 and Definition 2.1.5, pp. 810--811, 821--822; explicit support compression

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-adjunction-two-block-splicing] to each fixed pair of endpoint signs. The two block maps there are exactly restriction to vertices $\{0,\ldots,m\}$ and $\{m,\ldots,m+n\}$, by the formula for $I$ in step 3. Its condition $R(v_*a)=R(t_*b)$ is equality of the last vertex of the first block and first vertex of the second. Thus the restriction $W_{m+n}(x,y)\to W_m(x,y)\times_{W_0(x,y)}W_n(x,y)$ is bijective for all $m,n\geq1$. Iterating with $n=1$ identifies every simplex uniquely with its consecutive edges.

source.place: Proposition 3.2.2, pp. 824--825, using the isolated two-block splicing lemma

proof.text: For clarity, recover the hom-category directly from step 7. Its objects are $W_0(x,y)$, morphisms are $W_1(x,y)$ with the face endpoints, identities are $s_0$, and the composite of consecutive edges is the long edge $d_1$ of their unique spliced $2$-simplex. The unique $3$-simplex on a triple of consecutive edges gives equality of the two composites by $d_1d_1=d_1d_2$; the degenerate $2$-simplices give both unit laws. The spine bijections identify $W(x,y)$ with the ordinary nerve of this category: interior faces compose consecutive edges, outside faces drop an edge, and degeneracies insert an identity. Horizontal composition is a functor on these hom-categories, since it is simplicial and hence carries a composing $2$-simplex to the composing $2$-simplex. Thus $W$ is the homwise nerve of a strict $2$-category.

source.place: Proposition 3.2.2 and Recall 3.2.1, pp. 824--825; category and nerve reconstructed explicitly

proof.text: The only nondegenerate atomic $0$-arrows are $\ell=(-,+)$ and $u=(+,-)$: there are no internal numerical letters. In degree $1$, an atom can use the letter $1$ at most once, because there is no other internal letter with which it could alternate. The only nondegenerate ones are $\eta=(+,1,+)$ and $\epsilon=(-,1,-)$. Direct reduction gives $d_1\eta=1_+$, $d_0\eta=u\ell$, $d_1\epsilon=\ell u$, $d_0\epsilon=1_-$. For $\beta=(-,2,1,+)$ its faces are $(-,+,1,+)=\ell\eta$, $(-,+)=s_0\ell$, and $(-,1,-,+)=\epsilon\ell$, in orders $d_2,d_1,d_0$. The reflected string $\alpha=(+,1,2,-)$ similarly witnesses $(u\epsilon)(\eta u)=1_u$. Since a nerve triangle says its long edge is the composite, both triangle identities hold in the recovered strict $2$-category.

We show the required universal property, rather than assuming that a graphical model is the free adjunction. Let $K$ be any small strict $2$-category with an adjunction $L:B\to A$, $U:A\to B$, unit $e$ and counit $c$ satisfying both triangle identities. Larger $K$ is treated in a containing universe. Assign these data to $\ell,u,\eta,\epsilon$. Steps 5--6 give unique assignments in degrees $0$ and $1$ by taking words and degeneracies. They respect composition, faces and degeneracies there because each atomic $1$-arrow has the boundaries computed in step 9. The only remaining requirement for a map into a hom-category nerve is that every $2$-simplex boundary is a compositional triangle, by the edge-and-triangle presentation and nerve adjunction of [lem-coef-homotopy-category-nerve-adjunction]. We verify that requirement explicitly in steps 11--13.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.4, pp. 827--828; existing categorification/nerve leaf replaces the coskeleton extension

proof.text:
The nondegenerate atomic $2$-arrows have interiors alternating between $1$ and $2$, with each occurring. Write $\alpha_t$ for the one with target $+$ and $t\geq2$ interior letters, starting at $1$, and $\beta_t$ for its reflection (target $-$, starting at $2$). There are no other possibilities by strict alternation. Write $\eta_r:1_+\Rightarrow(u\ell)^r$ and $\epsilon_r:(\ell u)^r\Rightarrow1_-$ for the horizontal products of $r$ copies, including identities at $r=0$; these are not vertical powers. Apply the three collapsing alphabet maps and delete pairs. The faces $(d_2,d_1,d_0)$ are
$$\alpha_{2r}:(\eta_ru,s_0u,u\epsilon_r),\quad \alpha_{2r+1}:(\eta_{r+1},\eta,u\epsilon_r\ell),$$
$$\beta_{2r}:(\ell\eta_r,s_0\ell,\epsilon_r\ell),\quad \beta_{2r+1}:(\ell\eta_ru,\epsilon,\epsilon_{r+1}).$$
Here $r\geq1$. These formulas follow letter by letter: $d_1$ merges the alternating interior into a run of length $t$, giving no internal letter for even $t$ and one for odd $t$; $d_0$ and $d_2$ merge every other turn with the corresponding extreme and leave the displayed repeated unit/counit words.

source.place: Example 3.1.11, formula (3.1.12), pp. 822--823; reflected family made explicit

proof.text:
In $K$ let $e_r:1_B\Rightarrow(UL)^r$ and $c_r:(LU)^r\Rightarrow1_A$ be the same horizontal products. Put $A_r=(Uc_r)\cdot(e_rU)$, using right-to-left vertical composition. The base cases are $A_0=1_U$ and $A_1=1_U$ (the triangle). Interchange, with $e_{r+1}=(e_rUL)\cdot e$ and $c_{r+1}=c_r\cdot((LU)^rc)$, gives
$$A_{r+1}=(Uc_r)\cdot((UL)^rUc)\cdot(e_rULU)\cdot(eU)=A_r\cdot(Uc)\cdot(eU)=A_r.$$
Indeed the middle two factors commute past one another by the interchange axiom, giving $((UL)^rUc)\cdot(e_rULU)=(e_rU)\cdot(Uc)$. Also
$$(Uc_rL)\cdot e_{r+1}=(A_rL)\cdot e=e.$$
Thus all $\alpha_{2r}$ and $\alpha_{2r+1}$ boundaries map to compositional triangles, not just $\alpha_2$.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 3.3.4, middle-four computations, p. 828; base and inductive equations expanded

proof.text:
For the other family put $C_r=(c_rL)\cdot(Le_r)$. The base cases are $C_0=1_L$ and $C_1=1_L$, the other triangle. Use $e_{r+1}=((UL)^re)\cdot e_r$ and $c_{r+1}=c\cdot(c_rLU)$, so $Le_{r+1}=((LU)^rLe)\cdot(Le_r)$ and $c_{r+1}L=(cL)\cdot(c_rLUL)$. In $(LU)^rL$ the cell $c_r$ acts on the first $2r$ factors and $Le$ on the final $L$, so by the interchange axiom both $(c_rLUL)\cdot((LU)^rLe)$ and $(Le)\cdot(c_rL)$ equal the horizontal composite $c_r*(Le)$. Hence
$$C_{r+1}=(cL)\cdot(c_rLUL)\cdot((LU)^rLe)\cdot(Le_r)=(cL)\cdot(Le)\cdot(c_rL)\cdot(Le_r)=C_1\cdot C_r=C_r.$$
(The other expression $c_{r+1}=c\cdot(LUc_r)$ would not do here: its $c_r$ overlaps the factor $U$ created by $e$.) The same expression $c_{r+1}=c\cdot(c_rLU)$ gives
$$c_{r+1}\cdot(Le_rU)=c\cdot(C_rU)=c.$$
Consequently the even and odd $\beta$ boundaries also map to triangles. A degenerate atomic $2$-arrow gives an identity triangle. Every other $2$-arrow is a horizontal word of these, by steps 5--6; interchange says the horizontal product of compositional triangles is compositional. This verifies every triangle relation required in step 10.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 3.3.4, dual triangle calculation, p. 828; both parity cases expanded

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-homotopy-category-nerve-adjunction] to each $W(x,y)$. Its category $\tau W(x,y)$ is generated by vertices and edges modulo precisely the degenerate-edge and triangle relations verified above, so the assignments define functors $\tau W(x,y)\to K(Fx,Fy)$ and hence unique simplicial maps $W(x,y)\to N K(Fx,Fy)$. The product comparison $\tau(S\times T)\cong\tau S\times\tau T$ in the same leaf shows preservation of horizontal composition: the two induced functors on $\tau(S\times T)$ agree on vertices and edge generators by the word assignments of step 10, hence agree. Identities agree on their constant generators. The maps therefore constitute a simplicial functor. Conversely any such functor is forced on all $0$- and $1$-arrows by the unique word decompositions; the nerve adjunction then forces it on each whole hom-space. Since the hom-spaces are nerves (step 8), this is a strict $2$-functor. We have proved existence and uniqueness for every adjunction in $K$.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.4 and Corollary 3.3.5, pp. 827--828; extension justified using the existing Mathlib leaf

proof.text: Let $F$ be the free strict $2$-category specified in the item. The adjunction in $W$ gives a unique generator-preserving strict $2$-functor $F\to W$, by the defining universal property of $F$. Step 14 applied to the adjunction of $F$ gives a unique generator-preserving strict $2$-functor $W\to F$. Each composite fixes the adjunction generators and is therefore the identity by the respective uniqueness properties. Applying ordinary nerves to the inverse hom-functors gives the required isomorphism of simplicial categories. Its images of the four generators and $\beta$ are exactly step 9; the nerve triangle with those two consecutive edges is unique. All the combinatorial conclusions of steps 5--6 therefore apply to the specified nerve-enriched free adjunction.

source.place: Corollary 3.3.5, p. 828; inverse universal-property maps written explicitly

proof.text: A nondegenerate nonidentity $n$-arrow has at least $n$ interior positions, because every numerical letter occurs. A string of width $w>0$ has $w-1$ interior positions, so $n\leq w-1<w$. For any fixed positive $w$, this allows only $0\leq n\leq w-1$, and for each $n$ there are at most $(n+2)^{w+1}$ strings before imposing the endpoint and alternation conditions. The finite sum of these bounds proves finiteness over all dimensions. At width zero only the two singleton strings in degree zero are nondegenerate. This proves the last clause including that edge case.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 4.2.15, p. 838; explicit finite bound and identity exception
